May 1972 (US) | recorded = 1971 | studio = | venue = | genre = * Soft rock * pop | length = 3:36 | label = MAM | writer = Gilbert O'Sullivan | producer = Gordon Mills | prev_title = No Matter How I Try | prev_year = 1971 | next_title = Ooh-Wakka-Doo-Wakka-Day | next_year = 1972 | misc = {{External music video|header=Music video|{{YouTube|wR0hIUlxdcQ|"Alone Again (Naturally)"}}}} }} "Alone Again (Naturally)" (or "Alone Again") is a song by Irish singer-songwriter Gilbert O'Sullivan. Recorded in 1971, it became a worldwide hit. The song did not originally appear on his 1972 studio album Back to Front, but has been included in reissues (often replacing "Clair"). The single spent six non-consecutive weeks at number one on Billboard's Hot 100 between late July and early September 1972 in America. It ranked number two in the year-end chart and sold over two million copies. The song was involved in a notable 1991 court case in which it set a precedent for the music industry that unauthorized sampling of music can constitute copyright infringement.

sections.heading: Lyrics
sections.wikitext: "Alone Again (Naturally)" is a melancholic, introspective [[ballad]]. In the first verse, the singer contemplates suicide after having been left at the altar; in the second, he wonders why God let bad things happen; finally, he laments the death of his parents. O'Sullivan has said the song is not autobiographical: for example, his mother was alive during its composition, and he was not close to his father, who was abusive to his mother and died when the singer was 11 years old.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.superseventies.com/1972_2singles.html |title="Alone Again (Naturally)" - Gilbert O'Sullivan |website=Superseventies.com |date=1972-07-29 |access-date=2016-10-06}}</ref>

In the first verse, the singer contemplates suicide after having been left at the altar; in the second, he wonders why God let bad things happen; finally, he laments the death of his parents. sections.heading: Musical structure
sections.wikitext: Despite being essentially a pop ballad, the song has musical structure and harmony atypical for pop songs. It contains three verses and a bridge, with no chorus, as every verse ends with the song's title line, "Alone again, naturally". The verses are in the key of F{{music|#}} major and the bridge (positioned after the first two verses) changes the key to A major before returning to F{{music|#}} major for the third and final verse. The song has a relatively complex harmony using chords and progressions more common in jazz than in pop music, such as [[Half-diminished seventh chord|half diminished]] and flat [[ninth chord]]s. The piano technique used on the song is typical to O'Sullivan's playing style with a percussive bass note on the left hand and the chord changes on the right.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext: The song received extensive radio airplay in the months after its release and was critically praised. O'Sullivan commented: “[[Neil Diamond]] covered 'Alone Again (Naturally)' and said he couldn't believe a 21-year-old wrote it, but for me it was just one song I had written.”<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.advertiser.ie/galway/article/96322/i-can-still-compete-with-anyone-despite-being-around-so-long|title='I can still compete with anyone despite being around so long'|last1=Kernan|last2=Andrews|website=Galway Advertiser|access-date=26 January 2019}}</ref> [[Neil Sedaka]] stated when he covered the song in 2020 that he wished that he himself had written the song, because its complexity was more typical of someone much older than 21.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hgMFdNUZG2o |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/hgMFdNUZG2o |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live|title=Today's Mini-Concert - 10/22/2020|date=22 October 2020 |access-date=22 April 2021|publisher=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

sections.heading: Certifications
Copyright lawsuit
sections.wikitext:
{{Main|Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records Inc.}}

''Grand Upright Music, Ltd v. Warner Bros. Records Inc.'' was a [[copyright]] case heard in 1991 by the [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York]]. The case pitted O'Sullivan against [[Biz Markie]], after the rapper [[Sampling (music)|sampled]] O'Sullivan's song "Alone Again (Naturally)". The court ruled that sampling without permission can be copyright infringement. The judgment changed the [[hip-hop music]] industry, requiring that music sampling be preapproved by the original copyright owners to avoid a lawsuit.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.princeton.edu/~artspol/studentpap/undergrad%20thesis1%20JLind.pdf| title=Music Sampling and Copyright Law | page = 21}}</ref>
sections.text:
{{Main|Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records Inc.}}

Grand Upright Music, Ltd v. Warner Bros. Records Inc. was a copyright case heard in 1991 by the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. The case pitted O'Sullivan against Biz Markie, after the rapper sampled O'Sullivan's song "Alone Again (Naturally)". The court ruled that sampling without permission can be copyright infringement. The judgment changed the hip-hop music industry, requiring that music sampling be preapproved by the original copyright owners to avoid a lawsuit.

sections.heading: Cover versions
sections.wikitext: * Dutch comedians [[Kees van Kooten]] and [[Wim de Bie]] covered the song as ''1948'', also known under the title ''Toen was geluk heel gewoon'' (''Back then, happiness was a simple thing''). In the lyrics, they nostalgically reflect on their childhood in the late 1940s. The song became a hit in a version by [[Gerard Cox]] (and featured on his 1972 album ''Vrijblijvend...'', meaning ''No-obligation...'').<ref>[https://www.nporadio2.nl/muziek/nummers/acc23176-b144-4f8b-a61c-240b86043a5c/1948 NPO Radio 2 - 1948 - Gerard Cox]</ref> It later served as inspiration for the sitcom starring Cox and frequent collaborator/ex-wife [[Joke Bruijs]] that ran from 1994 to 2009, ''[[Toen Was Geluk Heel Gewoon]]'' (a Dutch adaptation of the short-lived mid-1950s US sitcom ''[[The Honeymooners]]''), which was the longest-running sitcom in the Netherlands.
